lines: A star with an unseen companion never sits still.
Here is what Gaia actually measures, built up one motion at a time.
This is the orbit of a classical binary pair: a Sun-like star and a one point four solar mass companion that emits no light, six hundred days around each other, five hundred parsecs away.
Both circle their common centre of mass. From a point moving along with the system, the star traces this ellipse.
Its size on the sky is called a zero: two point two milliarcseconds here. It grows with the companion's mass, and that is what makes the companion weighable.
But this is not how they look on the sky, because the Earth, and Gaia with it, are not stationary in space. Gaia rides with the Earth around the Sun.

Even a single star with no companion looks like this in Gaia's eyes: as Gaia circles the Sun, the star appears to circle too, once a year. That is the parallax ellipse, two milliarcseconds wide at five hundred parsecs.
Now give the star its companion. Orbit and parallax add, and the path becomes this rosette: a yearly loop that never repeats, because the orbit takes six hundred days.
Stars also move through the Milky Way, on orbits different from the Sun's. Seen from here, that adds a steady drift: the proper motion.
Over Gaia's five years the drift carries the star about fifty milliarcseconds, twenty times the size of the orbit.
The orbit is now a small wiggle on a nearly straight line. This is the true path of the star on the sky.
Gaia does not even see this path. It spins, sweeping its field of view across the sky, and each time the star crosses that field, Gaia records one number: how far along the sweep the star is.

Across the sweep it learns almost nothing. So one crossing only says: the star is somewhere on this line. Sixty-two crossings in five years, in ever different directions, each good to five hundredths of a milliarcsecond.
The fit must find the one combination of parallax, proper motion and orbit that passes through all of them.
Do that, and the orbit's size and period together with the parallax give the companion's mass: one point four solar masses, with no light from it at all.
That is how a dark companion is weighed.
